approved: Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Cost Recovery) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would let the government charge fees for environmental assessments under the EPBC Act.
Fees would be set in regulations, except for assessments by an inquiry or strategic assessment, which the minister would determine.
The bill also creates a formal process for action management plans, allowing fees to be charged when a person submits a plan after approval.
Allows cost recovery for environmental impact assessments and strategic assessments.
Lets regulations specify fees, administrative requirements, payment processes, refunds, exemptions and waivers.
Permits a person to elect to submit an action management plan after the minister approves the action.
Allows fees for assessing and approving action management plans and their variations.
People and organisations that submit environmental impact assessments, strategic assessments or action management plans under the EPBC Act.

Moved the second reading of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Cost Recovery) Bill, allowing cost recovery for environmental impact assessments, noting the measure was originally announced in the previous Labor government's last budget and accepted by the then opposition before the election.

Moved a second reading amendment on the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Amendment (Cost Recovery) Bill 2014 criticising the government's environmental record, and cited a February 2014 article in the UK's Independent newspaper asking whether the Abbott government is the most hostile to its nation's environment in its history.

Defended the government's one-stop shop environmental approvals reform, targeting bilateral agreement on approvals within 12 months, dismissed the shadow minister's claim of environmental atrocities as baseless rhetoric, and noted youth unemployment in North Adelaide, in the shadow minister's home state, has reached 20 per cent.

Defended the cost recovery bill, noting Labor itself included this measure in its 2013-14 budget for a 1 July commencement, said the one-stop shop reform will typically save businesses 30 to 40 business days, and criticized past federal intervention in a Dawesville Catholic Primary School oval expansion 3,000 kilometres from Canberra.

Criticised the proposed 100,000 hectare Tasmanian World Heritage extension covering forests worked for over 150 years, said adjoining private landowners were never consulted, and noted the World Heritage Committee's advisory body raised concerns about a lack of consultation with the Tasmanian Aboriginal community, addressed only by a promised half a million dollars.

Criticized the one-stop shop reform as trashing 40 years of cooperative federalism on the environment, noting this is the first time in 40 years there is no intergovernmental forum or standing committee dealing with environment and water.

Defended the one-stop shop reform as fulfilling Labor's own April 2012 COAG commitment, aiming to cut the average 720-day approval process to nine months, and framed the cost recovery bill as needed given the $240 billion debt inherited from the previous government, announcing a newly published agreement with Western Australia.
